messages.subject: ranked() function in NIBMLE
parts:
Hello team, 
I have been writing a ranked function for NIMBLE to implement posterior predictive checks, the one from Bugs works in the following way:
ranked(x,s) brings the s smallest component of v.

The idea is to sort the values of x and bring the s value that is of interest. 

The sort function is: 
Sort.Func<-nimbleFunction(
  run=function(X=double(1)){
    X<-X[!is.na(X)]
    N<-length(X)
    if(N>1){
    for(M in 1:(N-1)){
      for(I in 1:(N-M)){
        if(X[I]>X[I+1]){
          temp<-X[I]
          X[I]<-X[I+1]
          X[I+1]<-temp
        }
      }
    }
    }
  return(X)} )

In the code is just used once as is show below:

code <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:facility) {  
    b.Facility[i]~dnorm(mu.F, tau.F)
    sort.b.Fac[i]<-Sort.Func(b.Facility[1:facility])[i]
    ..... #some extra code ....

Once I load the model via nimbleMode I get the following warning: 
     Warning message:
     In code[[2]] == names(dimensionsList):
       longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length
Once I compile the model I get the following error:
     Error in sizeIndexingBracket(<environment>, new("symbolTable", .xData = <environment>),  : 
       Error in 'rcFun_R_GlobalEnv21(X=Interm_129)[getNodeFunctionIndexedInfo(ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__,1)]'; 
       has 'rcFun_R_GlobalEnv21(X=Interm_129)' been created?

I guess that during the comparison of the sorting function I am comparing 2 different sizes of vector and therefore is bringing the warning message. 
Is there something that I am missing in the code or the nimble function that it does not make it work??

Thank you in advance for your time :)

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: ranked() function in NIBMLE
parts:
Hi Diego,

Thanks for sharing with sufficient detail to see what is going on.

Can you please try the following:

Add returnType(double(1)) in the run function of Sort.Func.  That's a return type declaration (a numeric vector) so it is not evaluated as a line of code and can go anywhere.

Change the use in model code to:
sort.b.Fac[1:facility]<-Sort.Func(b.Facility[1:facility])
(outside the for loop)

Since you are returning a vector, it needs to be assigned to a vector.  If you want to pick out a scalar, it would be better to pass i as an argument to Sort.Fun and use returnType(double(0)) to return a scalar (rather than pick it out with [i] later, which I'm not sure will work but might).

For efficiency, non-scalars in compiled code are passed by reference.  This is very un-R-like.  In your case, you will want to copy X in Sort.Func before sorting it.

Model nodes cannot change size, so X<-X[!is.na(X)] may be problematic if you do not know in advance how large the intended return object is.  It might work well to keep the return object the same length as X and put any NAs at the end.

In your previous message, I may not have followed, but it looked like maybe you wanted to use the ranked() idea to get the smallest and largest values.  If that's the case, min or max would work. 

I hope that gets you closer to what you need.

-Perry

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: ranked() function in NIBMLE
parts:
Hi Diego,

Thanks for continuing with this.  There are several things going on.  In a nutshell, the compiler doesn't currently support NA very thoroughly.  This has come up in a couple of contexts recently, so I have drafted better support for it and have a draft pull request on our GitHub repository, which is running our test suite at the moment.

One reason we haven't supported NA very deeply through the compiler is that, in a model, it's not clear whether one really wants to be handling NAs in functions and distributions.  A common role for NAs has been to mark missing data when creating a model, which one wants to be sampled via MCMC, so that during MCMC operation the values are not actually NAs.  If there are NAs permanently in place in other variables in a model, often one would work around them in the model code, such as by using nested indexing to exclude any cases with NAs.  You probably have a good reason for wanting to handle them, but it might be worth thinking about avoiding them entirely.

If you do need to use NAs and want to do it in your own code similar to Sort.Func, what I suggest at the moment is establishing a protocol to use some non-possible number as your proxy for NA.  Another option would be to use NaN instead of NA.  You can assign NaN to a double (e.g. X[i] <- NaN).  Compilation does not support vectorized is.nan, so you would have to check for NaNs in the input vector (X) one by one in a for loop.  However, see below for a possibly more appealing solution.

It may be that we should add support for sort and rank for nimbleFunction compilation, but here is a way you could do it that simply calls R's C implementation of sort and thus achieves its handling of NAs, which is to put them at the end.  This is basically the same scheme as we used for the Bessel I function in another recent post on this list.  I know it is somewhat obscure to see what R's C headers expose for this kind of step, but they are in the includes directory of an R installation.  Here is the trick:

library(nimble)

sink('external_sort.h')
cat('
extern "C" {
 void R_double_sort(double *x, int n);
}
')
sink()
sink('external_sort.cpp')
cat('
 #include <R.h>
 #include "external_sort.h"
 void R_double_sort(double *x, int n) {
   R_rsort(x, n);
 }
')
sink()
system2("R", c("CMD", "SHLIB", "external_sort.cpp")) ## Ignore the .so (or .DLL).  We will use the external_sort.o
R_double_sort <- nimbleExternalCall(function(x = double(1), n = integer()) {},
                                    Cfun =  'R_double_sort',
                                    headerFile = 'external_sort.h', ## see note about paths belo2
                                    returnType = void(),
                                    oFile = 'external_sort.o')
## Because this will work by passing x by reference and having that as the sorted result,
## we need to wrap it in another layer.
nfsort <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    y <- x
    R_double_sort(y, length(y))
    return(y)
    returnType(double(1))
  }
)
## Check if it works by compiling it as a stand-alone nimbleFunction
cnfsort <- compileNimble(nfsort, dirName = ".")
cnfsort(c(1, 3, 2, 5, 4)) ## It works
cnfsort(c(1, 3, NA, 5, 4)) ## It works with NA going to the end

## Use it in a model
demoCode <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:5] <- nfsort(x[1:5])
})
demoModel <- nimbleModel(demoCode, inits = list(x = c(1, 3, NA, 5, 4)),
                         check = FALSE, calculate = FALSE) ## Can't calculate in R with a nimbleExternalCall
CdemoModel <- compileNimble(demoModel, dirName = ".")
CdemoModel$z
CdemoModel$calculate("z")
CdemoModel$z
## A note about paths.  I recommend something like headerFile = normalizePath(file.path(getwd(), 'external_sort.h'))
##  and similar for oFile.
## This is important when compiling the model, which is not by default done in your local directory.
## An alternative, which I've used above, is to give local paths to hearderFile and oFile
##   and then use dirName = "." in compileNimble for the model, which makes it use your local directory
##   for the C++ files.
## On my system, this avoided problems with a space in getwd() due to "Google Drive", but those are
##   just OS details.

In summary, your two best options are: Use NaN instead of NA and do not expect vectorized behavior of is.nan(X) to work correctly.  Or use the nimbleExternalCall I've given above.

-Perry
